name: Cerasee (bitter melon) tea
what_people_do: Boil the vine leaves of cerasee (Momordica charantia) and drink the bitter tea, for "sugar" (diabetes), colds, skin and as a cleansing tonic.
why_they_say_it_works: It is bitter, so it is "strong medicine"; it is believed to lower blood sugar and clear the system.

documented_by.source: Mahabir D, Gulliford MC 1997, Rev Panam Salud Publica, PMID 9128111
documented_by.quote_or_summary: 622 people with diabetes in Trinidad: bush medicines used by 42%, for diabetes by 24%; "caraili" (bitter melon), aloes, olive-bush and seed-under-leaf were preferentially used for diabetes; Afro-Trinidadians used bush medicine more than Indo-Trinidadians.

documented_by.source: Picking D et al 2015, J Ethnopharmacol, PMID 25929450 (TRAMIL survey, Jamaica)
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Jamaica TRAMIL survey of 407 adults (cerasee is one of the island's commonly cited plants in the agent4 reading; plant-by-plant figures not read).

3 users describe drinking cerasee tea in Jamaica. (1) Taught by a grandmother who gave it a few times a year, saying too much would cut your pressure. (2) Drank it about three times a week growing up. https://www.reddit.com/r/jamaica/comments/b2mvmz/ (3) mixes cerasee with sweet iced tea. Forum evidence documents use only; the tier is unchanged.

evidence.tested: Bitter melon vs placebo and vs metformin or glibenclamide in type 2 diabetes
evidence.population: 4 RCTs, 479 adults, up to 3 months (not diaspora-specific)
evidence.finding: No significant difference from placebo on glycaemic control; "insufficient evidence"; trials at high risk of bias.

source.name: Ooi CP et al 2012, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, PMID 22895968

harm_note: Bitter melon can lower blood sugar; people on diabetes tablets or insulin using it alongside risk going too low (general pharmacology, not found in the Cochrane abstract). MSK says safety data are sparse (agent4).
gaps: Dose and preparation of home teas differ from trial extracts.
